articles.headline: Counting Is the Occupation of the New York Canvassing Board. Nothing Definite Yet, and the American Nation, Like Patience on a Monument, is Anxiously Awaiting the End.
articles.text:
The only bulletins received here from the canvassing board are in relation to the vote of Queens county, where Cleveland's plurality is cut down from 1957 to 1952, and a general bulletin to the effect that the official canvass of over thirty counties has not materially changed the result.

This makes the whole matter as clear as mud for the reason that no one seems to know what that result was or is.

Both sides, as represented by papers and officials of the contending parties, claim the election and all must be contented with this until the official canvass is completed.

The result now hinges on New York state and it is confidently expected that inside of twenty-four hours the result will be known.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy reports the presidential election still undecided, hinging on the New York canvass.

articles.text: Northern Pacific bonds sold yesterday as follows: Common, 17¾; preferred, 47½.
articles.summary: Quotation of Northern Pacific securities.

articles.text: It is hard to catch Jay Gould napping. The Union Pacific railroad owes the government a large amount for which it has not been pressed under republican rule. Under democratic rule Thurman will probably be secretary of the treasury, and as he has already shown his hostility to the Union Pacific, as a subsidized road, the wily Jay, as soon as Cleveland's election seemed probable, sold all his Union Pacific stock. This will cause trouble about the control of the Oregon Railway & Navigation lines, but it is very probable that they will again be operated in connection with the Northern Pacific.
articles.summary: Editorial on Jay Gould selling Union Pacific stock and the outlook for the Oregon Railway & Navigation lines.

articles.text: It is singular what vaporings fill the [editorial?] mind of some newspaper correspondents, and what a mass of trash newspapers will use as "filling." We allude particularly to the discussion now going on relative to the division of this tier of counties in such a way that the eastern part of Billings county shall be merged into Stark county, and enough of Morton county set off so that Glenullin can be a county seat. The plan contemplating the still farther division of Billings county is one originated by a few disgruntled politicians without influence, money or common sense who hope to put a streak of county official fat over their impoverished skeletons. The original limits of Billings county have twice been contracted to make room for Dunn and Villard counties, and the only change that will be made is to restore to us our originall boundaries. As long as the Cow Boy is in its present hands, a county office in Billings county will be no place for a rascal who expects to fatten on his fellow citizens, and this very class that is now agitating division will find it very warm work to hold office here with their present lax ideas of morality. We have given more space than we ought to these political sharks, and have done with them until they "shtep on the tail o' me coat" to a little more purpose.
articles.summary: Packard denounces a proposal to split Billings county, merging its eastern part into Stark county, and vows the Cow Boy will oppose the agitators.

articles.headline: Thanksgiving Proclamation
articles.text:
Executive Office, Bismarck, Dak., Nov. 8, 1884.

In accordance with the proclamation of the president, I do hereby designate Thursday, the 27th day of November, as a special day of thanksgiving unto God for the blessings and mercies of the past year, and do recommend that the people of Dakota observe that day. For health, abundant crops, the preservation of life, freedom from great calamities; for progress in material things, for intellectual advancement, for a peaceful land and a prosperous nation, let the people meet at the altar and fireside and reverently give thanks unto the power that has blessed and preserved us.

And let us pray that war and pestilence, famine and flood may still pass this people by; that righteous judgments and prudent counsels may prevail in all our borders, to the end that law and order may reign, and public tranquility continue throughout the land.

Gilbert A. Pierce, Governor.
articles.summary: Governor Gilbert A. Pierce's proclamation naming Thursday, November 27, as Thanksgiving Day in Dakota.

articles.headline: Stock Notes. The Ranchman's Song.
articles.text:
In saddle or in camp at home,
I fear not fortune's change;
My wealth the branded herds that roam
The green wastes of my range!
Oh, who more independent, free,
And care exempt than I?
Not he that sails upon the sea
Or scales the mountain high.
I laugh and sing, give fancy wing,
And let the world go by.

The bustle of the run, the count,
The round-up and the drive,
Is pastime keen, if but the mount
Be mettled and alive.
Belted and spurred, devoid of fear,
To every risk resigned,
My cowboys [illegible] [reck?] career
As [headlong?] [as?] the [wind?];
Nor robber greed nor mad stampede
Can them unguarded find.

At work or play, with care to cause
No honest heart a pang,
And governed but by honor's laws,
On broncho or mustang,
Oh, who with more undaunted brow
Doth fell adventure bide?
Not he that speeds the pen or plough
Or stems broad traffic's tide!
In manhood's flower the plains I scour,
A ranchman true and tried!

Firm ward the mountain sentries keep
O'er my domain for me;
Far as the coursing gaze can sweep,
And rolling as the sea,
That cattle dotting realm expands,
Whence far abroad is strewed,
Rich nourishment for peopled lands,
The boon of wholesome food,
To mine the choice to here rejoice
Amid the solitude.

The saddle is my throne, the vast
Wild herds my vassals tried.
The lariat's swift, unerring cast
My mandate undefied.
My spurs were won by stubborn deeds
That ne'er a blush can bring,
Nor other, right or sanction needs
The care-free cattle king!
And joy brims up his stirrup-cup
In this the song I sing.

—[Exchange.
articles.summary: Reprinted poem 'The Ranchman's Song' heading the Stock Notes column.

articles.text: A colored cow boy at the Mobeetie festival, roped and tied down a steer in one minute and thirteen seconds. This is the best time on record for that feat.—[Exchange.
articles.summary: Clipping on a steer-roping record at Mobeetie.

articles.text: As the branding season is about over it is evident that the year's calf crop has been light. The cows in the early spring lost their calves, and now in the beef gathering it is difficult to determine which are the barren and which are not.—[Col. L. S. Record.
articles.summary: Clipping on a light calf crop.

articles.text: Frosts have recently visited various portions of the range during the past week, and will cause the stock men to rest easy so far as Texas fever is concerned. The "scare" upon this subject has already almost entirely disappeared, but, as frost is said to be the real exterminator of the disorder, its presence will drive out all fear that may have existed.—[Cheynee (Wyo.) Live-Stock Journal.
articles.summary: Clipping on frost ending Texas fever fears.

articles.text: A leaf of suet and kidney taken from a beef steer one day last week weighed 33 pounds. The butcher who dressed the animal states that in all his experience in butchering, which has been large, he has never seen this equalled, not even in corn-fed beeves in the states. The animal was a four-year-old steer raised on Smith river, and weighed 1,200 pounds when dressed.—[Miles City S. G. Journal.
articles.summary: Clipping on a heavy Smith river steer.

articles.text: An exchange thinks that western stockmen who buy young eastern stock cattle must be prepared to shelter them the first winter from the severe storms. No greater mistake can be made than to compel unacclimated calves and ill-conditioned yearlings to rustle for themselves and have no shelter from the wintry storms.
articles.summary: Advice on sheltering eastern stock cattle their first winter.

articles.text: M. W. Angle, living twenty-five miles south of Mingusville, sustained a serious loss Monday. His flock of sheep was stampeded over a bluff by a herd of cattle, and about 300 were killed. The coolie was filled with the bodies of the sheep, and the cattle used them as a bridge in crossing the coolie.
articles.summary: M. W. Angle lost about 300 sheep when cattle stampeded them over a bluff south of Mingusville.

articles.text: The five horse thieves arrested a few days ago near Miles City are to be taken to Regina, in the Canadian northwest. They stole $12,000 worth of horses form the Bell farm near there. The officers of Custer county will take them to the Canadian boundary and deliver them to the mounted police.—[Fort Benton (Mont.) Press.
articles.summary: Clipping on horse thieves to be returned to Canada.

articles.text: A reliable British authority has it that sheep will consume about fifteen pounds of dry and mixed food per week for each 100 pounds live weight. This, of course, when fattening for the shambles. The same authority says they should yield about one pound increase for every nine pounds dry food consumed. "Moderately fat sheep should yield 58 per cent. carcass in fatted live weight, and excessively fat sheep 64 per cent. or more."
articles.summary: Note on sheep feeding rates.

articles.text: The receipts of fat cattle and hogs at Chicago have been large of late and may be expected to continue large for some weeks to come. The percentage of fair to good quality arriving will naturally increase, as large numbers are now being fed feed freely. The range cattle may be expected to come forward freely. We see no room to expect an advance in prices, and possibly there may be a decline. The better grades of cattle will doubtless continue in the best request, but it may be questioned whether it will be wise to hold those already well ripened, and while there has been a somewhat discouraging fall in the price of hogs we certainly should not hold those already fully fat in hopes of any considerable advance in prices.—[Breeder's Gazette.
articles.summary: Clipping on the Chicago fat-cattle market outlook.

articles.text: A floating item says that the best horse doctor is a sensible horse. Give him liberty and he will take care of himself. Whoever saw a horse running wild troubled with the "heaves." A nibble at a poplar pole, or a bite of rosin weed and a full supply of grass is all he wants to put himself in a sleek, plump, happy condition. But if kept up and fed musty hay and made subject to the unnatural demands of a thoughtless owner, it is no wonder he suffers. Father Clarkson says "rosin weed" is a sovereign remedy for heaves, and any one who has seen the intelligent horse stretch his nose over to brouse it in the uncut grass when hitched to the mower, has evidence in support. A good horse is his own doctor if you give him a chance.
articles.summary: Item on horses doctoring themselves on the range.

articles.text: Frequently of late we have heard the cow boys complain that the work on the range now is not what it used to be; and this reminds us that down in Tenos and out in New Mexico and Arizona, the same complaint is made, and the Sidney (Tex.) Independent, speaking of this, says: "Cow boys don't have as soft a thing as they did eight or ten years ago," remarked one of the fraternity. "I remember when we sat around the fire the winter through, and didn't do a lick of work for five or six months of the year, except to chop a little wood to build a fire to keep warm by. Now we go on the general round-up, then the calf round-up, then comes haying—something that the old-time cow boy never dreamed of—then the beef round-up and fall calf round-up, and gathering bulls and weak cows, and after all this a winter of feeding hay. I tell you times have changed. You didn't hear the sound of a mowing machine in this country ten years ago. We didn't have any hay, and the man who thinks he is going to strike a soft job now in a cow camp is woefully left."—[Barber Co. (Kan.) Index.
articles.summary: Item, noting local cowboys' complaints, on how range work has grown harder.

articles.text: A very observing cattle breeder is Mr. Tuttle, of the Powder river country in Wyoming. Meeting the gentleman on the rotunda of the St. James the other evening, the Record engaged him in conversation on the bovine subject and the national trail, said he: "Up as far north as I am the people will have no use for this trail that you are advocating. I believe we have got all the Texas cattle that we need. The day is now on when a better breed of cattle will take their place. If there is no Texas cattle then there will be no fever, and if there is no fever then our northern cattle will be permitted to go down through Canada to the sea shore and out to Europe. And if there were no more broadhorns there would be more shorthorns and Herefords, and more beef, and more value in our herds. The four-year-old ox that comes over from Oregon will weigh an average three hundred pounds more than one of the same age up from Texas, and when fatted will put on a far greater per cent. of flesh. This is from the fact that the people of Oregon have been breeding up, while the Texans have been breeding down. No sir, we need no more Texas blood on our Wyoming heath. We need a race of cattle that should belong to the northwest. And I believe they will be produced by a cross with the shorthorns and the Herefords. Let them be called 'the North Cattle,' every steer of which at five years of age should weigh fifteen hundred pounds. These cattle will answer for export feeders, and will do credit to an English stall. A Texas steer with his broad horns would fright the yeomanry of their senses, and would only do to put on exhibition as a wild beast from the pampas of America."—Colorado L. S. Record.
articles.summary: Clipping: a Wyoming breeder opposes the national cattle trail and urges shorthorn-Hereford crosses.

articles.summary: Hotels are busy.

articles.summary: C. W. Sleeper left for Helena.

articles.summary: Levi Deffebach left for the Black Hills.

articles.summary: Auditor Sharkey continues examining the express books.

articles.summary: A thousand wethers are being slaughtered.

articles.summary: Cattle shipping season on the N.P. is nearly over.

articles.summary: Chicago prices for wintered Texans and Montana steers.

articles.summary: A freighting outfit left with Black Hills freight.

articles.text: Howard Eaton, Wm. Dantz and Ferris & Merrifield are engaged in a beef round-up.
articles.summary: Eaton, Dantz and Ferris & Merrifield are on a beef round-up.

articles.text: Superintendent Deffebach started on a tour of inspection of the stage line yesterday morning.
articles.summary: Stage superintendent Deffebach began an inspection tour.

articles.text: Superintendent Green started for Mandan this morning. He has been here several days on railroad business.
articles.summary: Railroad superintendent Green left for Mandan.

articles.text: Misses Mary and Annie Brophy return this evening to their home in Mingusville. We hope to see them here often.
articles.summary: The Misses Brophy return home to Mingusville.

articles.text: Orrin Kinley returned Tuesday from work on the stage route, and reports the line as being nearly ready for winter. He starts back to-day to complete the work.
articles.summary: Orrin Kinley reports the stage line nearly ready for winter.

articles.text: One of J. C. Fisher's buildings is nearly completed, and will be occupied in a few days by Mr. Cook. J. D. Garver will occupy the other as soon as completed.
articles.summary: J. C. Fisher's new buildings to be occupied by Cook and J. D. Garver.

articles.text: [illegible] track is being raised and improved. Considerable difficulty has been experienced in getting cars up the grade, which this change will obviate.
articles.summary: Track improvements to ease a grade; opening words hidden by a paper fold.

articles.text: John Kelly and wife, who have won a reputation on the Pacific slope as accomplished musicians, will give an entertainment here a week from to-morrow evening. Full particulars in our next issue.
articles.summary: Musicians John Kelly and wife to give an entertainment.

articles.text: Johnny Goodall has brought up five hundred stock cattle of the N. P. R. C. Co., and is holding them four miles below on the river. They are to be sold, as the company intends dealing exclusively in beef cattle.
articles.summary: N.P.R.C. Co. stock cattle held for sale as the company turns to beef cattle only.

articles.text: Bob Roberts expects to start in two weeks for New Orleans, to stay until spring. After that he will go to Wales to receive a legacy left him there by his father, and during the summer he will return to Medora.
articles.summary: Bob Roberts plans to winter in New Orleans and visit Wales.

articles.text: Hereafter receipts will be given to purchasers of coal from the Medora coal mine. The receipts can be obtained at the Cow Boy office, and cash in advance will be charged. Customers will please remember this rule.
articles.summary: Coal from the Medora mine now sold for cash with receipts from the Cow Boy office.

articles.text: Dr. H. M. Jorgens arrived Tuesday from Spearfish. He will make a most valuable citizen, and has come to stay. He intends immediately increasing his drug stock, and will carry everything necessary for a first-class drug store.
articles.summary: Druggist Dr. H. M. Jorgens arrives from Spearfish to settle.

articles.text: A new station has been built on the stage line between South Moreau and Indian Creek, and will be called Antelope. The stock is steadily improving, and schedule time must be lowered as the coaches are constantly beating it.
articles.summary: New Antelope station built on the stage line.

articles.text: There are still twenty-one cattle strayed from the car loads that were wrecked west of here. Five dollars reward for each head is offered by the railroad company, but they are not by any means meek-eyed states cattle, and it probably will be some time before they are all rounded up.
articles.summary: Railroad offers reward for 21 cattle strayed from a wreck.

articles.text: Changes are coming thick and fast in the railroad employes here. Kelly has gone to Dickinson, and his place has been taken by L. W. Anderson. Ives is in Sentinel Butte, and S. P. Elverson has his place as night operator, and Mr. Maxwell, formerly in the car accountant's office in Mandan, exchanges places to-day with agent Fegan.
articles.summary: Turnover among Medora railroad employees.

articles.text: Great sport was had at the opening night of roller skating in Robert's hall. One gallant swain, while skating with a lady companion, observed that a nail was not driven home in the floor and proceeded to amend the defect with the end of his back bone. He afterward acknowledged that he would have felt much better if his partner had also fallen.
articles.summary: Roller skating opens in Robert's hall.

articles.text: Johnny Munro has a calf, given him by Howard Eaton, and thereby hangs a tale; not tail, as will be seen. Johnny asked some round-up boys to brand the calf, and they did so. They grubbed both ears and the tail, wattled the fore-head, dew-lapped the brisket, and branded JOHN on one side and MUNRO on the other. No tenderfoot will pick up that calf for a maverick.
articles.summary: Round-up hands brand Johnny Munro's calf with his name.

articles.text: The dance last Thursday evening in Robert's hall was largely attended, and all enjoyed themselves thoroughly.
articles.summary: Well-attended dance in Robert's hall.

articles.text: E. E. Ball, of Mandan, a first-class dentist, will be here the last three days of next week to do any work in his line that may be required by our citizens.
articles.summary: Mandan dentist E. E. Ball to visit.

articles.text: The stage arrivals from the Hills so far this week have been as follows: K. W. Kinneer, Mrs. N. P. Rodebank, Harry Rodebank, Jos. Browning, John S. Allen, G. A. Eleson, George Wager and Jacob Rodenhaus.
articles.summary: Passengers arriving by stage from the Black Hills this week.

articles.text: There is no better opening in the country for a shoe and harness maker than at Medora. Work in these lines has been accumulating for a long time and there is enough at all times to keep two men busy. Who will be the first to take advantage of the opportunity?
articles.summary: Medora needs a shoe and harness maker.

articles.text: One of the Texas steers that escaped from the wreck, wandered upon the coal mine butte and out on the roof of the dug-out barn located on the east side. The roof caved in and the steer was effectually corralled, and only discovered yesterday. Sam English found him and intends roping him, tying the rope to the hind axle of a wagon and towing him into town. Medora has not yet been blessed with a circus, and we advise our readers to turn out immediately and see this one. It will probably last as long as the wagon does.
articles.summary: An escaped Texas steer falls through a dug-out barn roof on the coal mine butte.

Freighters Attention! — take your watch to the King jeweler, Spearfish or Deadwood, for repairs.
Drugs and Medicines — Dr. H. M. Jorgens, Medora, Dak.; complete stock on the corner of Third avenue and Third street.
Mayville Stock Farm, Mayville, Traill Co., Dak. — Mayville herd of Short Horns; J. L. & E. B. Grandin, Props.; W. W. Warren, General Manager.
Hardware and Tinware at J. D. Garver's, Little Missouri, Dak. — all kinds of tin and sheet-iron articles made and repaired.
Northern Pacific Railroad — "Going East or Going West"; St. Paul to Portland, Ore., Yellowstone National Park; Horton chair cars Duluth–Brainerd; Chas. S. Fee, General Passenger Agent, St. Paul, Minn.
General Store of the N. P. R. C. Co., Medora, Dakota — groceries, dry goods, ready-made clothing, hats, caps, canned goods, harness, saddles, tobacco and cigars, felt shoes, overshoes, boots and shoes, flour and feed; "Hunters Outfits a Specialty"; wholesale and retail.
Medora Stage & F. Co., A. T. Packard, General Manager, Medora — horse brand Y-bar (cut) on left shoulder; horses strung on stage stations between Medora and Deadwood; $25 reward for information on anyone dealing unlawfully with these horses.
Supply Depot for Milwaukee Beer, by the case, keg or car load — C. B. Williams & Co., Bismarck, Dak.
E. J. Owenhouse, Bozeman, Mont. — stock saddles, Concord harness, fancy bits and spurs, chaparejos, reatas, quirts, hackamores.
Minneapolis & St. Louis Ry, "Famous Albert Lea Route" (map ad).
Wise & Goodkind, Bismarck, Dak. — wholesale dealers in wines, liquors, cigars; case & bar goods.

Brand: Dorr Clark, Spearfish, Dakota — V V V on left side; ear mark under-bit in left ear; range Belle Fourche.

Brand: Pennell & Roberts, P.O. Medora, Billings Co. — RR and JP horse brands for horses and mules; ranch four miles down river from crossing of N. P. R. R. and Little Missouri.
Brand: Lydia S. Fuller, Frank S. Moore, Manager, P.O. Medora, Billings Co. — LSF on left shoulder; range O'Donnell creek.
Brand: Custer Trail Cattle Co., F. Alden Eaton, Supt., P.O. Medora, Billings Co. — HK in circle on left side; 2nd and 3rd brands; horse brand T over V on left hip; range Little Missouri river, Deep and Davis creeks.
Brand: Towers & Gudgell, P.O. Keith, Montana — O X on right side; additional brand V on both sides; range south of N. P. R. R., on Little Missouri river and Beaver creek.
